abstract.text:
We study empirical scaling laws for language model performance on the cross-entropy loss.
The loss scales as a power-law with model size, dataset size, and the amount of compute
used for training, with some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude. Other
architectural details such as network width or depth have minimal effects within a wide
range. Simple equations govern the dependence of overfitting on model/dataset size and the
dependence of training speed on model size. These relationships allow us to determine the
optimal allocation of a fixed compute budget. Larger models are significantly more sampleefficient, such that optimally compute-efficient training involves training very large models
on a relatively modest amount of data and stopping significantly before convergence.

abstract.text:
We study empirical scaling laws for language model performance on the cross-entropy loss.
The loss scales as a power-law with model size, dataset size, and the amount of compute
used for training, with some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude. Other
architectural details such as network width or depth have minimal effects within a wide
range. Simple equations govern the dependence of overfitting on model/dataset size and the
dependence of training speed on model size. These relationships allow us to determine the
optimal allocation of a fixed compute budget. Larger models are significantly more sampleefficient, such that optimally compute-efficient training involves training very large models
on a relatively modest amount of data and stopping significantly before convergence.

identity.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models

evidence.quote: One might expect language modeling performance to depend on model architecture, the size of neural models, the computing power used to train them, and the data available for this training process.
In this work we will empirically investigate the dependence of language modeling loss on all of these factors, focusing on the Transformer architecture [VSP+17, LSP+18].

question.text: How does language modeling loss depend on model architecture, model size, training compute, and dataset size, and can these dependencies be described by predictive power laws and used to allocate compute optimally?

references.title: Which algorithmic choices matter at which batch sizes? insights from a noisy quadratic model

relations.quote: A simple empirical theory for the batch size dependence of training was developed in [MKAT18] (see also [SLA+18, ZLN+19]).
relations.why: The paper adopts the critical batch size and gradient noise scale model to define Smin and correct compute trends.

relations.quote: We train language models on WebText2, an extended version of the WebText [RWC+19] dataset, tokenized using byte-pair encoding [SHB15] with a vocabulary size nvocab = 50257.
relations.why: The WebText dataset and tokenizer supply the training and test corpus for all scaling experiments.

relations.quote: We primarily train decoder-only [LSP+18, RNSS18] Transformer [VSP+17] models, though we also train LSTM models and Universal Transformers [DGV+18] for comparison.
relations.why: The Transformer architecture is the primary model family whose scaling laws are characterized.

relations.quote: We also compare the performance of standard Transformers to recurrent Transformers [DGV+18] in Figure 17 in the appendix.
relations.why: Recurrent Universal Transformers are a comparison architecture for parameter reuse and compute trade-offs.

relations.quote: Note, however, that [HNA+17] found super-linear scaling of dataset size with model size, whereas we find a sub-linear scaling.
relations.why: Its super-linear data-scaling result is directly opposed to this paper's sub-linear D ∝ N^0.74 finding.

relations.quote: EfficientNet [TL19] advocates scaling depth and width exponentially (with different coefficients) for optimal performance of image models, resulting in a power-law scaling of width as a function of depth.
relations.why: The paper contrasts its finding that language-model shape is relatively unimportant with EfficientNet's architecture-specific scaling recipe.

relations.quote: Overfitting should be related to the variance or the signal-to-noise ratio of the dataset [AS17], and this scales as 1/D.
relations.why: The 1/D overfitting intuition from this prior work is extended into the paper's empirical L(N,D) scaling law.

relations.quote: Independence of nlayers would follow if deeper Transformers effectively behave as ensembles of shallower models, as has been suggested for ResNets [VWB16].
relations.why: Its ensemble hypothesis motivates the explanation for weak dependence on Transformer depth.

relations.quote: Our results on optimization, such as the shape of learning curves, can likely be explained using a noisy quadratic model, which can provide quite accurate predictions [ZLN+19] in realistic settings.
relations.why: The noisy quadratic model is proposed as a possible explanation for the observed learning-curve power laws.

relations.quote: Very recent work [RRBS19b] studies scaling with both dataset size and model size for a variety of datasets, and fits an ansatz similar to ours.
relations.why: This concurrent work fits a similar scaling ansatz, reinforcing the paper's scaling-law findings.

source_span.end_text: Taken together, these results show that language modeling performance improves smoothly and predictably as we appropriately scale up model size, data, and compute.

sections.summary: Introduces the empirical scaling-law problem and previews the main findings: performance depends strongly on scale, weakly on shape; power laws span many orders of magnitude; overfitting and training speed have simple equations; larger models are sample-efficient; optimal compute use favors large models and early stopping.
